messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Carlos is a 75-year-old married Latin American man who worked for decades as a QA engineer before retiring last year. Fifteen years ago, a fast-moving wildfire swept through his suburban neighborhood while he was late at the office, running one more diagnostic test. By the time he got home, his street was closed and his house—the one he and his wife had saved for their entire marriage—had collapsed into a smoking pile of ash and melted siding. His wife had escaped with the dog, but that was all they had left. In the months that followed, Carlos would replay that day endlessly: *If I had left work earlier, if I hadn’t been so meticulous, if I had insisted we install a sprinkler system*. He came to believe that his own thoroughness—the very trait that made him a good engineer—had cost him everything.

Now, years later, the smell of smoke still stops him cold. A neighbor’s barbecue will send his heart hammering before he even registers the scent, and he finds himself gripping the kitchen counter, breath shallow, scanning for flames. On hot, dry, windy days—weather that mirrors the afternoon of the fire—he becomes jumpy and watchful, checking the sky for plumes. That hypervigilance makes him notice even the faintest whiff of smoke or the flicker of a candle across the restaurant, which then triggers another wave of physical reactivity: his chest tightens, his hands tremble, and he has to excuse himself from the table. The physical symptoms themselves—the racing pulse, the sense of dread—lead him right back into the same old rumination. He will sit in his parked car, thinking about how he should have pushed his wife to leave earlier, how he should have read the weather forecast more carefully, how the whole disaster could have been prevented if only he had been more attentive. He tries to push those thoughts out of his mind—telling himself *Stop, just stop*—but the more he suppresses, the more the images intrude. And the ruminations make him more alert to potential triggers: while driving home on a windy day, he catches himself scanning the roadside for smoke, bracing for a repeat of that afternoon.

Carlos’s wife has grown used to seeing him freeze at the sound of a smoke alarm or the sizzle of a frying pan. At a recent family picnic, someone burned a couple of hamburgers on the grill; the smell sent Carlos straight into a spiral of self-blame about the fire, and he spent the rest of the afternoon in the car, windows up, trying not to think. He knows his reactions are excessive, but he cannot shake the conviction that danger is always one careless moment away. That same logic makes him avoid the news during wildfire season and refuse to drive past the rebuilt houses in his old neighborhood. The avoidance has cost him: he turned down a consulting project because the office building had an open-flame fireplace in the lobby, and he has not been able to enjoy the retirement he and his wife planned. What finally brought him to therapy was a morning three weeks ago when a neighbor’s leaf-blower sent a plume of dust into the air; Carlos smelled dirt and dry leaves, dropped to the ground, and hyperventilated for ten minutes. His wife begged him to get help. Carlos agreed because he is afraid—more afraid than he admits—that if he does not fix this, he will spend whatever years he has left trapped in the smoke of a day that already passed.
